newsitem.title: THAILAND: Mixed fortunes seen for Thailand from weaker baht.
newsitem.headline: Mixed fortunes seen for Thailand from weaker baht.

text.p: The baht's dive to a 56-month low against the dollar will bring mixed fortunes for Thailand's economy, analysts said on Thursday.
Some said the Thai currency's weakness against the dollar would hinder the inflow of short-term foreign funds due to concern over the possible foreign exchange losses.

"This (downward) trend will reduce the kind of portfolio inflows into Thailand. This is a worrying situation, given that this portfolio inflow has financed the Thai current account deficit," Desmond Supple, senior emerging markets economist at Singapore-based I.D.E.A, told Reuters.
The baht has been favoured by many Asian investors and speculators because of the high interest rate it offers.
But other analysts noted that because the baht was pegged to a basket of currencies dominated by the dollar, it had strenghtened against other majors such as the yen and mark.
Seamico Securities said in a report that the baht's strength against the yen would help ease Thailand's trade deficit which had worsened significantly over the past two years when the yen was strong.

But analysts said the baht's weakness would not significantly help boost Thailand's sagging exports because the sector was affected by structural problems. Last year Thailand posted zero exports growth after double-digit growth in 1995.
"We are not going to get an immediate benefit from the recent weakness (of the baht against the dollar) given structural problems in export sector," Supple said.
Teera Ashakul, the head of research department at Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand, agreed. He said the baht's appreciation against other major currencies would make it tougher for Thai exports.
He noted that Thailand's major export markets were the European Union, ASEAN countries and Japan, while the U.S. market represented less than one-fifth of the country's export market.
Supple said the baht's weakening against the dollar would not put pressure on domestic inflation because most of Thailand's imports were from Japan.
"The inflation potential of the baht weakness is negligible," he said. "Thailand's largest suppliers of imports are from Japan ...The overall import bill will actually decline."
In 1995, Thailand's imports totalled 1.76 trillion baht ($70.4 billion). Imports from Japan topped the list and were worth 538.7 billion baht.
A central bank official told Reuters on Thursday that there was no need for the Bank of Thailand to stop the baht's slide against the dollar.

"There is no need to take any action. Against other majors, the value of the baht has remained constant on a weighted average basis. It is only against the dollar that it has dropped," the official said.

Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said on Tuesday that his government had no plans to devalue the baht to boost exports and was happy with its value. "I don't believe in the assumption that baht devaluation is a quick fix for economic problems," he said.
The baht has fallen sharply against the dollar this week after the dollar's strength on overseas markets. The Bank of Thailand fixed the baht/dollar mid-rate at 25.67 on Thursday.
